verses.text: You are the children of Yahweh your God. You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead.
For you are a holy people to Yahweh your God, and Yahweh has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, above all peoples who are on the face of the earth.
You shall not eat any abominable thing.
These are the animals which you may eat: the ox, the sheep, the goat,
the deer, the gazelle, the roebuck, the wild goat, the ibex, the antelope, and the chamois.
Every animal that parts the hoof, and has the hoof cloven in two and chews the cud, among the animals, that may you eat.

Nevertheless these you shall not eat of them that chew the cud, or of those who have the hoof cloven: the camel, the hare, and the rabbit. Because they chew the cud but don’t part the hoof, they are unclean to you.
The pig, because it has a split hoof but doesn’t chew the cud, is unclean to you. You shall not eat their meat, and you shall not touch their carcasses.
These you may eat of all that are in the waters: whatever has fins and scales may you eat.
You shall not eat whatever doesn’t have fins and scales. It is unclean to you.
Of all clean birds you may eat.
But these are they of which you shall not eat: the eagle, the vulture, the osprey,
the red kite, the falcon, the kite after its kind,
every raven after its kind,
the ostrich, the owl, the seagull, the hawk after its kind,
the little owl, the great owl, the horned owl,
the pelican, the vulture, the cormorant,
the stork, the heron after its kind, the hoopoe, and the bat.
All winged creeping things are unclean to you. They shall not be eaten.
Of all clean birds you may eat.

You shall not eat of anything that dies of itself. You may give it to the foreigner living among you who is within your gates, that he may eat it; or you may sell it to a foreigner; for you are a holy people to Yahweh your God. You shall not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk.
You shall surely tithe all the increase of your seed, that which comes out of the field year by year.

You shall eat before Yahweh your God, in the place which he chooses, to cause his name to dwell there, the tithe of your grain, of your new wine, and of your oil, and the firstborn of your herd and of your flock; that you may learn to fear Yahweh your God always.

If the way is too long for you, so that you are not able to carry it, because the place is too far from you, which Yahweh your God shall choose, to set his name there, when Yahweh your God shall bless you;
then you shall turn it into money, and bind up the money in your hand, and shall go to the place which Yahweh your God shall choose.

You shall trade the money for whatever your soul desires, for cattle, or for sheep, or for wine, or for strong drink, or for whatever your soul asks of you; and you shall eat there before Yahweh your God, and you shall rejoice, you and your household.
You shall not forsake the Levite who is within your gates, for he has no portion nor inheritance with you.
At the end of every three years you shall bring all the tithe of your increase in the same year, and shall store it within your gates.

The Levite, because he has no portion nor inheritance with you, and the foreigner living among you, and the fatherless, and the widow, who are within your gates, shall come, and shall eat and be satisfied; that Yahweh your God may bless you in all the work of your hand which you do.

footnotes.content: Here Moses says what we so often forget: you belong to God first. That's your true name—not your job, not your shame, not your scar. The pagan world marked itself with cuts and scars in grief; Israel was forbidden from that. Your mourning doesn't have to carve you.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Chosen." Not because Israel earned it. Not because they were numerous or wise or strong—they were actually the smallest. God chose them the way a grandparent loves a particular grandchild: with no reason except the love itself. That same choosing reaches toward us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Abominable thing"—a short word that covers all the ways the world tempts us to swallow what hurts us. Holiness is sometimes just refusing to eat poison, even when you're hungry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The ox, sheep, and goat—the very animals Abraham knew and kept. Deuteronomy grounds covenant law in the stories God's people had lived. We are not starting over with strange rules; we are continuing a long conversation with God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The list of wild animals Israel could hunt—deer, gazelle, antelope—these would have been the feast of a careful, skilled hunter. Even in the boundary-drawing, there is room for the wild, the chase, the provision of one's own hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Cloven hoof" and "chews the cud"—two conditions, both required. The laws teach discernment: some things look acceptable from one angle but fail the other test. Wholeness requires checking more than one measure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The camel chews its cud but doesn't fully part the hoof. We know the camel—powerful, patient, suited to hard journeys. Even the good creature, examined closely, may not fit into this particular covenant shape. That's not a judgment on camels; it's clarity about boundaries.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The pig has the split hoof—looks clean—but chews no cud. The visual trickster. This law teaches that surfaces deceive. What appears acceptable on the surface may not align with deeper truth when you look inside.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fish with fins and scales—creatures with clear boundaries, adapted for the waters they swim in. The law keeps pointing toward this: integrity means fitting rightly into the shape God has made for you.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What has no fins and scales—the water-dwellers that slip through categories, that feel wrong in the hand. Some things carry their "unclean-ness" close to the surface, and wisdom is reading the signs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Clean birds may be eaten—a simpler rule for the sky-dwellers. Not every law is burden; some open a door. Manna-fed ravens, bread-carrying eagles, doves carrying peace—the birds sing in the space freedom allows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eagles—hunters of the sky, fierce and high. Even the noble creature, clothed in power, stands outside this boundary. The law is not a judgment on the eagle's worth; it is Israel's particular yes and no.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Red kite, falcon—the predators that stoop and strike. The law excludes the hunters, the flesh-eaters of the air. Israel is learning a shape for itself, and that shape does not include all appetites.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every raven—the carrion-eaters, the opportunists. The birds that feast on death are shut out from Israel's table. But notice: ravens appear again in the Psalms and Gospels as Fed by God's hand. Even the excluded bird receives grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ostrich, owl, seagull—birds of odd habit, creatures of dusk and desert. The world has room for such creatures. Israel simply draws its boundary elsewhere, saying: this is not the shape we choose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Little owl and great owl—the watchers of night, eyes wide in darkness. Different sizes, same nature. The law sees carefully, naming each creature in its particularity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pelican, vulture, cormorant—water-birds and scavengers, each excluded. The list grows long, patient, thorough. This is not a law thrown down in haste; this is a law that has looked at the world.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Stork, heron, hoopoe, bat—the stork was a bird of care (it tends its young long), yet still excluded. The bat hangs upside-down, a creature of reversal. These particular animals close a list, and the list is complete.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All creeping, flying things are unclean—the insects, the small winged creatures that swarm and multiply. The law draws one final boundary. Now the table is set; now Israel knows its yes and no.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This verse repeats verse 11—"clean birds you may eat." Repetition in Torah is not mistake; it is emphasis, a return to the open door after the long list of closures. After all the no, a reminder of yes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An animal that dies of itself is not for Israel to eat, but may be given to the foreigner or alien—an act of provision, not waste. And then, mysteriously: "You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk." This strange prohibition (repeated three times in Torah) resists easy explanation. Some say it was pagan ritual; some say it teaches gentleness. What matters: the law honors boundaries and mercy together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tithe—a tenth—the language of trust made visible. Not half. Not all. A tenth of the harvest, given year after year. You keep nine-tenths; the Lord keeps one-tenth. It is a simple mathematics of faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You shall eat before Yahweh your God, in the place which he chooses"—the tithe becomes a feast, a meal of gratitude. This is not extraction; this is covenant meal-sharing. The point is not the loss, but the communion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "If the way is too long"—the law anticipates real life, real distance, real hardship. The covenant does not demand the impossible. Grace is written into the structure itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Turn the tithe into money, carry it with you, and spend it where God's name dwells. Innovation within obedience—the spirit allows the letter to breathe. The point was never the physical grain; the point was always the giving.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Whatever your soul desires—cattle, sheep, wine, strong drink." The law permits joy. This is not a law of scarcity or denial; it is a law that invites a feast, celebration, the gladness of a household before the Lord. Your redemptive God wants you to eat well and rejoice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You shall not forsake the Levite." The Levites have no inheritance of land, no material anchor. Only covenant obligation holds them. The law turns toward the vulnerable and says: you are remembered. Your Lord sees you.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every three years, gather all the tithe and store it in your gates. This is another rhythm of faithfulness—not constant drain, but cycles of abundance and care. The God who made seasons also makes rhythms for the human heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Levite, foreigner, fatherless, widow—the four faces of the vulnerable. When we gather in gratitude and set a table wide enough for all, we echo something the Lord himself has done. Looking back from where I stand now, I see how many times He has welcomed me to His table when I had no claim on it but His kindness. Readers today hear an echo of that same grace when they choose to share.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
